name: Forpost-RU

placement_rationale.text: 7 km marks where Forpost-RU does its forward ISR/strike work, not the airfield its 1,150 kg, runway-dependent airframe actually launches and recovers from — a license-built Searcher derivative this large needs fixed ground infrastructure normally sited well to the rear, reached via its 250 km comms range rather than by operating close to that infrastructure itself. 7 km sits inside doctrine.md §2's drone-dense corridor (~30 km either side of the front), the same forward-operating convention applied to its Ukrainian counterpart (Bayraktar TB2) and to Orion in this same catalog, plausible for the reconnaissance-strike orbit this asset's own characteristics describe rather than for the rear airfield itself. (Nudged 7→6.6 km from this category's shared round-number value so it doesn't literally coincide with side_b-uav-orion on the map's distance axis — a small, deterministic spread within the same band, not a new plausibility claim beyond what's already argued above.)

characteristics: Strength: Largest and most expensive UAV in this catalog batch; long endurance and high-altitude operation
Limitation: Very high unit cost makes it the least numerous, most operationally cautious-to-risk type in the fleet
Estimated quantity available: Small fleet; exact total not disclosed
employment_notes: A license-built derivative of an Israeli design (IAI Searcher), illustrating that Russia's higher-end UAV fleet has historically depended partly on pre-war foreign technology transfer rather than fully domestic design
contrast_vs_traditional: A license-built derivative of an Israeli design, Forpost-RU is another case of existing airframe knowledge repurposed rather than a clean-sheet program — traditional procurement doctrine planning for a decade-long development cycle has given way, across this war, to adapting whatever design and supply chain is actually available on a wartime timeline.

notes: Specs meet the bar but the unit cost is an estimate — cost is not verified.
